criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural community and small-town drinking-water service access, borehole/handpump and piped system functionality, reliability, crowding, and household water consumption levels in Akatsi (North and South) and East Gonja districts, Ghana.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines decentralised rural water governance under Ghana's Community Ownership and Management (COM) model, District Water and Sanitation Plans (DWSPs), Medium Term Development Plans (MTDPs), District Composite Budgets, and the District Monitoring and Evaluation System (DiMES). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although general asset monitoring and routine physical maintenance Practices would alone resemble operational/project management, the study directly and empirically examines tariff and cost-recovery rules (comparing water point functionality across monthly levy, volumetric pay-as-you-fetch, and no-fixed-tariff / post-paid fix-on-failure regimes in Table 2; assessing volumetric tariff affordability; and evaluating compliance with the 2008 national model bye-law rule requiring small-town WSMTs to pay at least 20% of net monthly revenue into a capital account and CWSA cost-recovery rules splitting OpEx user fees from District Assembly CapManEx support), as well as decentralised service-provider governance structures (WSMTs) and non-enforcement of the CWSA Legislative Instrument (2007).
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods empirical study combining reanalysis of a baseline inventory dataset (371 handpumps and 160 service providers across Akatsi South/North and East Gonja districts collected Nov 2011–Jan 2012), review of district planning and budget documents, and primary fieldwork in Feb–Mar 2013 (21 semi-structured key informant interviews, 7 site visits, financial/administrative record inspections, 6 community/WSMT focus groups, and 2 area-mechanic focus groups).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service access outcomes: borehole/handpump and small-town piped scheme functionality and partial functionality (including stratified by tariff regime: 74% under monthly levy, 69% under pay-as-you-fetch, 50% under no fixed tariff), reliability (>18 days breakdown per year), basic service level attainment (crowding and CWSA standards), basic water quantity accessed (<20 litres per person per day for 39% in East Gonja and 49% in Akatsi), and tariff affordability.
criterion_notes.c5: Population, units of analysis (water point/handpump and piped system, community WSMT service provider, and district assembly service authority), exposures (tariff/cost-recovery regimes, model bye-law capital-account rules, routine maintenance, district budgeting/monitoring, and LI 2007 enforcement), outcomes, and mixed-methods study design are all clearly identified.

evidence_quotes.quote: These factors have had an impact on water consumption with 39% of residents in East Gonja and 49% of residents in Akatsi South and North failing to get basic access of at least 20 litres of water per person per day, according to Adank et al. (2013).

According to the national model bye-law, (MLGRDE, 2008) Water and Sanitation Management Teams for small towns are required to make a monthly payment of not less than 20% of their net monthly revenue to their capital account.
Two key and interrelated factors are identified: (1) tariff structure implemented by the community; (2) the routine maintenance of the infrastructure.
District staff, however, admit the lack of systematic monitoring and enforcement of the Community Water and Sanitation Agency Legislature Instrument (2007) are reasons for this occurrence.
21 semi-structured key informant interviews with a cross section of District Assembly and Community Water and Sanitation Agency Head Office and Regional staff
Moreover, between 30 and 40% of handpumps in both districts were broken down for over 18 days a year – thus failing to meet the reliability indicator (Moriarty et al., 2011; CWSA, 2014a).

raw_response.exposure: Tariff and cost-recovery rules/regimes (monthly levy vs volumetric pay-as-you-fetch vs no fixed tariff / post-paid fix-on-failure; national model bye-law requirement to deposit >=20% of net monthly revenue into a capital account; life-cycle cost allocation between user fees and District Assembly composite budgets), routine maintenance practices, decentralized Community Ownership and Management (WSMT) governance, District Monitoring and Evaluation System (DiMES) reporting, and enforcement of CWSA guidelines and Legislative Instrument (2007)
raw_response.outcome: Water system functionality and breakdown rates (service availability/continuity), service reliability (breakdown >18 days/year), attainment of CWSA basic service level standards, daily water quantity accessed (>=20 litres per person per day), and tariff affordability
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural small communities and small towns in Akatsi (North and South) and East Gonja districts, Ghana: secondary quantitative dataset of 371 handpumps and 160 WSMT service providers (Table 2 n = 253–254 community borehole/handpump systems), plus primary fieldwork comprising 21 key informant interviews (District Assembly and CWSA national/regional staff), 7 site visits, 6 community/WSMT focus groups, and 2 area-mechanic focus groups (4–5 participants per district). Units of analysis: water supply facility (handpump/piped scheme), community WSMT, and District Assembly.
raw_response.rationale: Full-text empirical mixed-methods study in rural Ghana examining how tariff and cost-recovery rules (monthly levy vs volumetric pay-as-you-fetch vs no fixed tariff / post-paid fix-on-failure; compliance with the 2008 model bye-law 20% capital-account rule; District Assembly budgeting for CapManEx/ExpDS), decentralized WSMT governance, district monitoring/planning frameworks, and non-enforcement of CWSA Legislative Instrument (2007) affect borehole/handpump and small-town piped water functionality, reliability (>18 days/year downtime), basic service levels, and residents' access to >=20 L/person/day. Satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods empirical study (cross-sectional quantitative reanalysis of facility and service-provider inventory dataset combined with policy/budget document review, semi-structured key informant interviews, site visits, and focus group discussions)
